summary: This is South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 25 for October 1947, prepared in Korea by the National Economic Board for USAMGIK. It opens with an editorial on poor integration among SKIG agencies and covers population and repatriation, vested property, food supply, prices, agriculture, mining, industry, trade, labor, public services, finance, government and politics, and social matters. The dominant concerns are the 1947 rice collection and the contested rice price, with a falling rice stock, a 30 October National Economic Board session and legislative wrangling over collection law. Politically it records the appointment of Maj. Gen. William F. Dean as Military Governor, the Russian troop withdrawal proposal, the general election and UN representation debates, leftist and rightist clashes, and the Korean National Youth anniversary. Historians will find dense statistical tables, import and allocation detail from the Civilian Supply Program, financial data, and records of Assembly proceedings and press opinion.
highlights: Maj. Gen. William F. Dean announced as Military Governor of Korea on 30 October 1947.
Summer grain collection reached 97.1 percent of quota: 1,237,576 hectoliters.
Rice selling price raised from 85 to 120 won per small mal; projected deficit 1.06 billion won.
Final 1947 rice estimate: 24,930,000 hectoliters brown rice.
Japanese alien registration counted 458,359 Koreans by 15 September; about 600,000 expected.
Korean National Youth membership reached 290,333 on 31 October.
Executive Order No. 8 of 20 October restricted rice transportation.
Prison population stood at 20,652 on 30 September 1947.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 25 (October 1947), prepared by the National Economic Board for the Civil Affairs Division, with blank and image-only pages. The contents list covers Part I Basic Aspects, II Production and Supply, III Public Services, IV Finance, V Government and Politics, and VI Social.

sections.title: Explanations and Implications
sections.summary: The editors call this the second monthly report produced wholly in Korea, with the format now settling and no charts yet pending drawings from SCAP. They say poor integration among SKIG departments, such as competing claims on electric power and bituminous coal, limits the report, and add that non-economic social controls strongly shape Korean behavior.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and vested property.

sections.title: Section 1: Population
sections.summary: Cumulative movement since 15 October 1945 shows 885,667 outbound and 2,342,852 inbound; 21,363 Koreans were caught trying to enter Japan illegally. Northern refugees continued at 9,661 in October. SCAP limited repatriation from Japan to illegal entrants, deportees and approved cases; 458,359 Koreans registered in Japan; Sakhalin Koreans petitioned for return.

sections.title: Section 2: Vested Property
sections.summary: The Office of Property Custody completed a Kangwon-do inventory of 56,730 pieces of former Japanese property. It surveyed textile plants for a 150 million won rehabilitation of 12 units, guaranteed six loans totaling 361,850,000 won, took in 21,967,085 won in October, advanced operating funds to three departments, and handled 161 Operations Division cases.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Food, prices, agriculture, mining, industry, distribution, trade and labor.

sections.title: Section 1: Food Supply
sections.summary: Summer grain collection finished at 1,237,576 hectoliters, 97.1 percent of quota, with Cheju-do at only 16.4 percent. Polished rice stocks fell from 1,851,049 hl in June to 434,955 in October. The 1947 rice quota was 5,156,000 suk; only 3.2 percent was collected by 5 November. Executive Order No. 8 restricted rice transport, and rationed population reached 9,476,856.

sections.title: Section 2: Prices
sections.summary: Rice prices set 15 September were published in October. The 30 October National Economic Board minutes defended the 640 won per bag purchase price and 120 won per small mal selling price, projecting a 1.06 billion won deficit. Seoul price indices, gold, and National Price Administration actions on coal, tobacco, tires and bicycles are also reported.

sections.title: Section 3: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: The final 1947 rice estimate is 24,930,000 hectoliters of brown rice, about 15 percent above 1946. Cotton fell to 42,125,574 kg after cool rains, and cocoon collection reached only 717,000 kg, 45.6 percent of goal. Also covered are livestock, a 967 million won irrigation budget, fertilizer sales at 82 percent of receipts, forestry and fisheries reporting.

sections.title: Section 4: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output rose to 32,395 tons in September against 21,043 in August, but stockpiles kept falling. The Yong Wol mine could reach 100,000 tons monthly with a 24-mile railroad. Bituminous coal from Japan was 64,588 tons in October, with sub-allocations set by the Production Board. Pitch is short, and tables give metals output.

sections.title: Section 5: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Output data mostly cover September: flour at 430.4 tons, up 83 percent, cotton yarn and cloth declining, and machine-made paper at 375.1 tons, the highest since November 1946. The Inchon welding plant began making nails. Onada cement fell 44 percent, firebrick fell 72 percent, and Monopoly Bureau ginseng, salt and tobacco are reported.

sections.title: Section 6: Allocation and Distribution
sections.summary: Explains how Commerce allocates Korean-produced goods by province (cloth, shoes, soap, matches, tires, beer, cottonseed oil), with 367 civilian supply allocations in September and 837 in October, including trucks, clothing, cement and dynamite. FFA spent 66,697,000 won in October and FDA sales to provinces reached 269,575,779 won. Petroleum drum deposits rose to 1,000 won; salt kimchi ration cut to 2.7 kg.

sections.title: Section 7: Import and Export
sections.summary: Private trade nearly balanced in October on permit estimates (270 million won imports, 283 million exports); September imports rose 8.45 times and exports 4.9 times over August. Covers barter and shipments with the U.S., Japan (SCAP open account), Hong Kong and Egypt, a new commercial shipping agency, Civilian Supply Program IV, and imports of 64,588 tons of coal, salt, fertilizer and foodstuffs.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: National Labor Week opened 20 October with lectures, contests and radio broadcasts; the Tai Han No Chong Labor College at Inchon was inspected, and the first Labor News and a union-meeting booklet appeared. Maximum-hours violations by two employers went to court; rightist and leftist unions contested Pusan seamen; a Seoul employee survey counted 59,009 workers; industrial health inspections covered about 15 plants.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities, public works and housing.

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: Department revenue rose 7 percent in September, helped by the 20 August freight-rate rise of 50 percent, while expenditures rose 18 percent. Railroad receipts rose 6 percent, passengers hit a fiscal-year high, freight tonnage rose 14 percent, and 55 percent of locomotives stayed inoperative. A Korean LST sailed to Shanghai; a three-day Pusan stevedore strike won a 29 percent handling-charge increase.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: Departmental revenue rose from 31.9 to 35.8 million won in September, with 12 million won misclassified as miscellaneous income, while expenditures rose 72 percent to 74 million won on winter provisioning. Staff fell 4,466 since April as insurance collectors went onto commission. Covers postal savings, the Postal Book Transfer System, insurance, telephone and telegraph, and a doubling of postal rates on 1 October.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Electric power delivered from North Korea rose 25 percent in October, to 55 million kWh of 80 million total. Seoul had 130 streetcars carrying about 500,000 passengers daily after repairs using Civilian Supply parts; 23 trucks were converted to busses in 1947. Power plants ran at reduced capacity for lack of water, and a welfare section was set up for Seoul Electric Company hospitals.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: Public works man-days (150,839) and wage expenditures (26.75 million won) in October reached their highest since May. Resurfacing of the Yong Dong Po to Si Hung highway began with asphalt; bridge designs for Kotong and Taehwang were finished. Han River to Ascom City pipeline repairs found 290 leaks; a Cheju-do water survey proposed wells and reservoirs; fire service chiefs met 19 October.

sections.title: Section 5: Housing
sections.summary: The National Housing Administration finished 11 prefabricated experimental low-cost houses at its Yong Dong Po factory. Findings shifted the design from 8 to 7 pyung with a kitchen and two sleeping rooms, and a forty-house project with Seoul City is planned. Refugee housing and tent winterization fall to Public Health and Welfare; the City of Seoul completed its 400-house project in October.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue rose almost 1.4 billion won in October to 21.8 billion, driven by rice collection and deficit spending; cumulative excess government withdrawals reached 19,859 million won. Collections ran at 75 and 72 percent of projected quarterly revenue. The 1947/48 budget stood at 18.79 billion won with 3.3 billion more requested; Civilian Supply receipts of 1.22 billion left a balance near 4.0 billion.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Cash balances in financial institutions rose 427 million won in September owing to rice-collection preparations, and deposit balances rose 3.6 billion to 34.4 billion won, with the Bank of Chosun holding 53 percent. Loans outstanding reached 14.3 billion won. Covers life and damage insurance, 12 billion won in credit lines for rice collection, silk credit, a November-December deposit drive and insurance company developments.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, legislature, politics, security, police, interzone activities and legal affairs.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: Hodge announced on 30 October that Maj. Gen. William F. Dean would become Military Governor. The section reprints Hodge's and Helmick's speeches at the Korean National Youth anniversary, reviews Civil Service divisions and training, notes Executive Orders 6 and 7, and records National Economic Board budget approvals and the 640-won rice price session.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: In 16 sessions averaging 66 members, the Assembly passed parts of the Temporary Administrative Organizational Law and an Ordinance No. 118 amendment, and forwarded Rhee's UN delegate petition 34 to 7. It debated rival rice collection laws, voted to rescind Executive Order No. 8, approved Lee Choon Ho as Seoul National University president, and read the entertainment-suspension bill.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: Politics centered on Rhee as UN representative, the timing of a general election, and the Russian withdrawal proposal. Rightists pressed for immediate South Korean elections; moderates formed the National Independence Federation under Kimm Kiu Sic. Release of the South Korea Labor Party's 15 August riot plan prompted demands to disband leftist groups, while the Laboring People's Party reorganized.

sections.title: Section 4: Internal Security
sections.summary: The Department of Internal Security comprises the Coast Guard and Constabulary. Constabulary men guarded supply areas, including the Pusan coal pile, and the Coast Guard's Pusan harbor block boarded 436 vessels in one week and 672 the next. Conferences addressed police friction with both forces, Constabulary recruiting screening, cost-of-living payments and terrorist youth groups.

sections.title: Section 5: Police
sections.summary: Police Director Chough marked the force's second anniversary and warned of the difficult rice collection. Rice law changes, including Executive Order No. 8 and citizen quota committees, aimed to curb past abuses. Other items covered Order No. 6 limits on business inspections, solicitation permits, women prisoners' clinics, Kangwon border shots, labor party arrests, rightist-leftist clashes and three murders.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: The US-USSR Electric Power Section handles goods paid for North Korean power; use from 16 August 1945 to 31 May 1947 was 837,678,737 KWH. At a 21-24 October Pyongyang conference payment was fixed in goods at controlled ceiling prices and future agreements to be signed by Koreans. Mail exchanged 18 October included 6,348 letters from the South.

sections.title: Section 7: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: The Department of Justice section covers air mail Order No. 19, Ordinance No. 150 on gold transactions and Executive Order No. 8 on rice transport. Legal opinions addressed press criticism of the Civil Administrator, Assembly vetting of appointees and legalizing a gold mining program. Prisoners numbered 20,652, and 54 of 700 applicants passed the bar.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Health, education, information, press and youth.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: A cholera outbreak in Sanchong had 14 cases and 6 deaths; September communicable disease and vaccine stock tables are given, with typhus control and rat-control plans. Other items: six leper clinics, nursing and dental figures, swine plague treated with sulfanilamide, refugee camp winterization, 19,707 refugee dwellings, milk plans, welfare training, and Women's Bureau work including ex-prostitute committees.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: Korean Alphabet Day was marked on 9 October. South Korea had 12,452 schools and 3,122,140 pupils, while textbook printing fell to 339,754 for lack of paper. The section covers Rockefeller and U.S. scholarships, Technological Training Board projects, nursing responsibilities, the Korea University incident, Seoul National University changes, and Cheju-do's severe teacher shortage.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Information
sections.summary: The Department of Public Information released 95 news items in October and printed one issue of Farmers Weekly because of newsprint shortage. Rice collection posters were prominent, and 1,060,000 copies of Hodge's letter on the UN proposal were dropped by air. It also reports seven information centers, 11 radio stations, film distribution to 65 theaters, and photographic panels.

sections.title: Section 4: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press debated the Russian troop withdrawal proposal, with moderate papers backing the U.S. line and leftist Dok Lib Sinbo praising the Soviet plan. Rhee's 18 October call for a South Korean election was quoted. Papers of most shades attacked the rice transport ban, and rightist papers publicized the 26 October Nam San rally and the 15 August plot report.

sections.title: Section 5: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Helmick's 20 October memorandum described Korean National Youth as an official non-political, non-military USAMGIK activity for ages 18 to 35, led by Lee Bum Suk. Membership rose from 157,218 on 31 July to 290,333 on 31 October. The 7-11 October anniversary drew over 300,000, with Seoul parades, and Taedong terrorism was reported.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Pages 328 to 333 are blank or nearly so. They hold only Google digitization notices, a library barcode number and a due-date slip stamped June 23 2010, with no report text.
